children: Last Friday's agreement by the G7 countries to

100M barrels of oil and diesel from emergency stocks aimed to curb high prices has received a largely muted response in the energy markets, with the oil price selloff appearing to lose steam, as confusion grows over how many barrels Europe and the U.S. plan to make available.

The announcement did ​not provide a breakdown of the volumes of crude, diesel, and other products to be released or say which countries ​would participate, but the governing board of the International Energy Agency—while it will coordinate the release of the fuels—is expected to reveal details at an October 14-15 board meeting, Reuters reported.

Analysts at Standard Chartered say the indifference of oil markets to the developments is because the 100M-barrel release is not a new emergency action but instead an acceleration of the original 400M-barrel release announced in March shortly after the start of the Iran war.

The market has known since March that up to 400M barrels would be made available, and only the urgency with which governments want the remaining commitments to be delivered has changed, Stanchart noted, adding an accelerated release can ease some near-term pressure but is not enough to address the underlying tightness in refined products and does nothing to resolve the disruptions and capacity constraints that created that tightness in the first place.

Avoiding a U.S. diesel export ban removes a major downside risk to European supply and is arguably as important as the stock release itself, Standard Chartered said, although the U.S. commitment only preserves existing supply flows without adding further supply.

LNG vessel traffic from Qatar through the Strait of Hormuz has increased since mid-September, which Stanchart sees as a positive signal after supply remained strictly limited through the summer, but the magnitude is not yet sufficient to support the notion of a meaningful supply recovery, and QatarEnergy's force majeure remains in place.

Meanwhile, U.S. diesel futures have edged higher after President Trump signed an executive order allowing temporary on-road use of dyed-red diesel with the corresponding federal excise tax deferred through the end of the year, but large trucking operators probably will not take advantage of the federal tax deferral for on-road use of dyed diesel given the complications, GasBuddy's head of petroleum analysis Patrick De Haan said on X.

"Interstate trucking means a patchwork of state rules and tax headaches, and most major truck stops don't sell dyed diesel," De Haan wrote, adding the deferral of the $0.244/gal excise tax will not change much at the pump for most diesel users.

On Tuesday, crude oil futures finished little changed after recouping earlier losses, as the market weighed increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz against a pickup in Iranian attacks against vessels.

While shipments through the strait have jumped in recent weeks, UK Maritime Trade Operations has reported at least nine attacks in the waterway so far this month, which is already half of the number recorded across Hormuz and the Persian Gulf combined last month.
